Thank you for watching the video. I will now make a statement as the President of the General Assembly. Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, dear colleagues, thank you for joining this 40th anniversary commemoration of the Declaration on the Right to Development. For me, this is also a deeply personal occasion. I was there 40 years ago during the 41st session of the General Assembly when this declaration was adopted. I remember that occasion. I remember the spirit of that moment, the sense, particularly among those furthest behind, that their voices had been heard, that their concerns could no longer be ignored, and that the vast disparity between developed and developing countries were not peripheral to this Assembly's work, but central to it. Forty years later, here we are, And the core message of that declaration remains as powerful and as necessary as ever, that every person, that all peoples have the right to participate in and contribute to and enjoy development. Development is not merely about economic growth. It is a comprehensive economic, social, cultural, and political process. It is about the constant improvement of human well-being through people's active, free, and meaningful participation, and through the fair distribution of its benefits. At its heart, the declaration affirms a simple truth. People must remain at the center of development as its participants, its beneficiaries, and its authors. Excellencies, The decades that ensued saw what is perhaps the greatest leap in human development in history. Global life expectancy has increased by nearly a decade. The likelihood of a child dying before their fifth birthday has fallen by 60%. And the likelihood of that child going to school has risen. Some 1.5 billion people have escaped extreme poverty. And a technology that did not even exist when this declaration was adopted now connects more than 5 billion human beings. Each of these figures represent something far more meaningful than a statistical gain or a simple number. A child lives longer and thrives. A young person learns. A family enjoys greater security, and a community gains new possibilities. Yet for all our successes-- and there have been many, and this organization has been quite central in ensuring them. Let's not forget that. Yet all for our successes, we also know that progress has been uneven across regions, within societies, and across development goals themselves. Indeed, only 36% of the 139 SDG targets are on track or making moderate progress. Many countries continue to face structural barriers, financing constraints, unsustainable debt burden, and unequal participation in global decision making. And 40 years after declaring development a right, far too many of these rights to education, to food, to a job, depend on factors beyond a person's control, determined by geography, by gender, by environmental conditions. So as we mark this anniversary, our task cannot simply be to celebrate the progress of the past 40 years. We must also reflect honestly on what those 40 years have taught us and act on those lessons. The first lesson, Excellencies, is that development must be inclusive. The declaration does not speak of passive beneficiaries. It speaks of participants and contributors. Development cannot be delivered to people from above. It must be shaped with them. It must empower the very people it aimed to support. That means ensuring that women and young people, marginalized communities, and those farthest behind have a meaningful voice in the decisions that affect their lives. And it means addressing the structural obstacles and historic and contemporary inequities that continue to constrain progress. Unequal access to finance, technology, and markets, limited fiscal space, and immense debt burdens that continue to constrain governments' ability to invest in their people. To be clear, closing the financing gap for sustainable development is not a peripheral concern. It is fundamental to empowering communities and thereby fulfilling the right to development. This is why the second pillar of my presidency is clear-- no one left behind, no country left out. We must restore faith in multilateralism by ensuring that it delivers for those who have too often been excluded from its benefits. The second lesson is that development is indivisible. It cannot be separated from human rights, from environmental concerns, and from peace and security. We see this today in countries where conflict wipes away decades of development in a matter of months. where human rights abuses undermine public confidence in justice and jeopardize social cohesion, and where debt burdens force governments to choose between servicing debt and investing in their people. These relationships also work in the other direction. When development gains falter or erode, when people lose access to decent work, education, food, and health care, to name a few, the social contract begins to tear. frustration grows, trust weakens, insecurity and instability deepens, and which in turn places human rights under serious and increasing pressure. The architects of the Charter understood this interplay, and it is for these very reasons that this document, the United Nations Charter, our foundation, is built on those three supportive and interactive pillars. Peace and security, development, and human rights. None can endure without the other. And the third lesson is that our understanding of development must evolve as our world evolves. The reality is that the world today is not as it was in 1986 when the declaration was dropped. Indeed, a few could have imagined the digital world we inhabit today. or the speed at which artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are now transforming economies, societies, and institutions. These technologies offer extraordinary opportunities to improve social services, expand access to quality education, create new jobs, and help accelerate progress towards sustainable development. But opportunity does not guarantee equity. The digital divide remains vast. While 68% of the world's population used the internet in 2024, 2.6 billion people remained offline. The respect, protection, and promotion of human rights, including the protection of children from Technology related harms, including potential adverse consequences arising from artificial intelligence, together with safety, transparency, accountability and meaningful human oversight, are essential considerations throughout the AI life cycle. Excellencies, Mr. Secretary General and friends, the right to development in the years to come will hinge on our ability to capitalize on and leverage these powerful new technologies, all the while mitigating the risks, which are many. That is why innovation with inclusion is one of the priorities of my presidency. We must bridge digital divides, build capacity in developing countries, and ensure that governance of new technologies is inclusive, transparent, participatory, and grounded in human rights and human security. Every country should have the opportunity not merely to consume the technologies of the future, but to help shape them. Excellencies, 40 years ago, this assembly elevated the notion of development from an aspiration to a right. There is power in these words. A right creates duties. It demands accountability. It requires that we measure progress not only by aggregate growth, but by whether people can live with dignity, exercise their rights, and shape their own futures. Today, let us honor the Declaration not only through commemoration, but through implementation. Let us protect the hard-won gains of the past four decades. Let us address the inequalities and structural barriers that persist. Let us make multilateralism more representative, more responsive, and more capable of delivering for all. The world has changed profoundly since 1986. Our commitment to the right to development must not. And I thank you. I now have the immense pleasure of inviting our Secretary-General to make his statement. I give you the floor, sir.

Of the development, human rights, and peace are not separate ambitions. They advance together. And in today's divided world, this vision can still unite us. Thank you, Mr. President of the General Assembly, Secretary General, excellencies, distinguished participants. The Declaration on the Right to Development clarifies and strengthens our shared work to achieve all three pillars of the United Nations, sustainable development, peace and security, and human rights. States agreed that they must empower every member of society to participate in decision-making and in the distribution of the benefits of development. Rooted in struggles against colonialism and exploitation, The declaration also emphasized states' commitment to dismantling structural inequalities in the global economy and to cooperation with each other in an environment of mutual respect. Because development is not about enriching an elite, and it cannot be measured by narrow focus on GDP alone. The goal of development is broad and transformative, to deliver greater freedom, human dignity, and well-being to every member of society. In fact, development as freedom was what Amartya Sen put forward in his book that awarded him the Nobel Prize. The 40th anniversary of adoption of the declaration calls for states to live up to their commitments by addressing three obstacles to its implementation. The first obstacle is that our international economic and financial systems are grotesquely out of balance. Unequal terms of trade and unbearable debt repayments squeeze human rights and human dignity out of public budgets. The burden falls heaviest on the most vulnerable members of society. It further heightens the inequalities that tower over the lives of hundreds of millions of people, crushing their rights and deepening their disenfranchisement through abject poverty. The second obstacle, the failure to alleviate human misery, is coupled with a seemingly insatiable competition for military, economic, and personal power. And The Secretary General yesterday in his address to the General Assembly dealt indeed with what power means in today's world. The declaration specifically calls for countries to disarm and to reallocate weapons budgets to people's development. But 2025 was the 11th consecutive year of increasing global military spending. It now amounts to some 2.8 trillion US dollars. That is eight times more than the estimated cost of ending extreme poverty globally. But strengthening peace and security depends on inclusive and sustainable development, which fulfills the rights and aspirations of ordinary people and builds social cohesion and resilience to shocks. It also rests on the creation of a fair and just international order, all of them key to the Declaration on the Right to Development. The third obstacle is that our economic systems and patterns of consumption are destroying the landscapes we live in, poisoning the air we breathe, and exterminating the species with which we coexist. Even the newest technologies have a voracious appetite for energy and scant regard for the scale of the environmental harm. We need a fundamental rethink of our approach to our economies and societies. Development must be equitable and environmentally sustainable. It cannot be equated to economic growth achieved at any cost to people and the planet. We need a strong shift towards greater equality, participation, dignity, freedom and mutual respect and we need to recommit to the principle of international cooperation, which is at the core of the right to development. The right to development is at the heart of sustainability. It is the basis of my office's work to promote human rights economies, which tackle inequalities and deliver greater well-being and hope for everyone. In fact, it is part of the mandate of my office. And it provides a sound foundation for states' consideration of future global development frameworks beyond 2030. And I encourage constructive engagement towards a legally binding instrument on the right to development. The Declaration on the Right to Development is a blueprint for strong, resilient, and truly inclusive societies that cooperate with each other in an environment of mutual respect. Let's come together around this anniversary year to reimagine development that delivers human rights for all. Thank you.
